items.stem: Which term describes a list of written questions completed by respondents themselves, by post, online or by hand?
items.answer: Questionnaire
items.markingKey: Questionnaire: a list of written questions completed by respondents themselves, by post, online or by hand. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “closed question”, and give one example.
items.answer: A question that offers a fixed choice of answers. Example: “Do you own your home? Yes / No”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a question that offers a fixed choice of answers); 1 mark for a relevant example such as “Do you own your home? Yes / No”. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “operationalisation” and “pilot study”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Operationalisation: turning an abstract concept into something that can be measured (e.g. measuring “religiosity” by frequency of attendance and prayer). Pilot study: a small-scale trial of a research method to identify problems before the main study (e.g. testing a questionnaire on ten people to find confusing questions).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: An interviewer in Jakarta reads a fixed list of questions about housework to husbands while their wives are in the room. Suggest how an interpretivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: pre-set questions impose the researcher’s meanings and cannot uncover respondents’ own interpretations, so the data lacks validity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: An interviewer in Jakarta reads a fixed list of questions about housework to husbands while their wives are in the room. Explain how an interpretivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: pre-set questions impose the researcher’s meanings and cannot uncover respondents’ own interpretations, so the data lacks validity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to research experiences of bullying in secondary schools.
items.answer: Strengths: a sympathetic, non-judgemental interviewer can help people talk about painful or private experiences; they produce rich, detailed qualitative data that gives verstehen (an empathetic understanding). Limitations: the power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear; the interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias). Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying experiences of bullying in secondary schools but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “closed question”.
items.answer: A question that offers a fixed choice of answers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a question that offers a fixed choice of answers. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “structured interview” and “closed question”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Structured interview: an interview in which the interviewer reads out the same pre-set questions in the same order to every respondent (e.g. a market research interviewer reading questions from a schedule). Closed question: a question that offers a fixed choice of answers (e.g. “Do you own your home? Yes / No”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why positivists favour questionnaires.
items.answer: Standardised so reliable; large, representative samples allow generalisation; quantitative data allows correlations and hypothesis testing; researcher detached so objective; cheap and quick.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Standardised so reliable; large, representative samples allow generalisation; quantitative data allows correlations and hypothesis testing; researcher detached so objective; cheap and quick. [8]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using semi-structured interviews to research experiences of bullying in secondary schools.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can adapt questions sensitively while still covering the key issues; the interviewer can probe and clarify answers, which improves validity. Limitations: interviewer bias may still affect answers; samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying experiences of bullying in secondary schools but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes an experiment carried out in a controlled, artificial setting where the researcher manipulates variables?
items.answer: Laboratory experiment
items.markingKey: Laboratory experiment: an experiment carried out in a controlled, artificial setting where the researcher manipulates variables. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “dependent variable”, and give one example.
items.answer: The factor measured to see whether it is affected by the independent variable. Example: the number of job interview offers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the factor measured to see whether it is affected by the independent variable); 1 mark for a relevant example such as the number of job interview offers. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “dependent variable” and “field experiment”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Dependent variable: the factor measured to see whether it is affected by the independent variable (e.g. the number of job interview offers). Field experiment: an experiment carried out in a real-life social setting, often without participants knowing (e.g. sending identical job applications with different names to employers).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Sofia, a researcher in Toronto, sends pairs of identical job applications to employers, one with a local-sounding name and one with a migrant-sounding name. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: experiments allow variables to be controlled so that cause and effect can be identified objectively and the study can be repeated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Leila, a researcher in Madrid, sends pairs of identical job applications to employers, one with a local-sounding name and one with a migrant-sounding name. Explain how a positivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Positivism: experiments allow variables to be controlled so that cause and effect can be identified objectively and the study can be repeated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating discrimination by employers against migrant job applicants. Evaluate the use of participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it records real behaviour, avoiding the gap between what people say and what they do; it is flexible and can uncover issues the researcher had not anticipated. Limitations: the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt; the researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”). Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying discrimination by employers against migrant job applicants but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “dependent variable”?
items.answer: The factor measured to see whether it is affected by the independent variable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the factor measured to see whether it is affected by the independent variable. [1]

items.stem: In a field experiment in Riyadh, researchers sent 120 pairs of identical job applications to employers. In each pair one used a locally common name and the other a name associated with a minority ethnic group. 48 of the “local-name” applications received an invitation to interview, compared with 42 of the “minority-name” applications. What is the difference between the two success rates?
items.answer: 5 percentage points
items.markingKey: 48/120 = 40%; 42/120 = 35%; difference 5 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Mohammed, a sociology student, is designing a project on the effect of teachers’ expectations on pupils’ progress. Explain one strength of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: It records real behaviour, avoiding the gap between what people say and what they do.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the effect of teachers’ expectations on pupils’ progress. [2]

items.stem: Which term describes numerical data collected by governments and their agencies?
items.answer: Official statistics
items.markingKey: Official statistics: numerical data collected by governments and their agencies. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “census”, and give one example.
items.answer: A survey of the whole population of a country, usually carried out every ten years. Example: a national population count recording age, household size and occupation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a survey of the whole population of a country, usually carried out every ten years); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a national population count recording age, household size and occupation. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “hard statistics” and “dark figure of crime”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Hard statistics: statistics that are relatively objective and difficult to manipulate, such as births and deaths (e.g. registered deaths). Dark figure of crime: crime that is not reported to or recorded by the police and so does not appear in official statistics (e.g. unreported domestic violence).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A researcher compares recorded crime in Madrid, which fell by 12% in one year, with a victim survey for the same year that shows little change. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Marxism: official statistics are produced by the state and may serve ruling-class interests, for example by concealing inequality or focusing on working-class crime rather than corporate crime.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Samuel uses official unemployment statistics to measure change in Bangkok over ten years, although the government changed the definition of “unemployed” during the period. Explain how an interpretivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: official statistics are social constructions produced by the decisions of officials and the public, so they tell us more about those decisions than about the reality they claim to measure (Atkinson, Cicourel).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the extent of domestic violence. Evaluate the use of unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: a sympathetic, non-judgemental interviewer can help people talk about painful or private experiences; the interviewee can raise issues the researcher had not thought of, so the research is not limited by pre-set categories. Limitations: they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare; each interview is unique, so it is hard to repeat and the data is less reliable. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the extent of domestic violence but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “official statistics” and “primary data”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Official statistics: numerical data collected by governments and their agencies (e.g. census data, crime figures and birth rates). Primary data: data collected first-hand by the researcher for the current study (e.g. answers from a researcher’s own questionnaire).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the extent of domestic violence. Explain two strengths of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. 2. Every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the extent of domestic violence. [4]

items.stem: Lucas uses official unemployment statistics to measure change in Colombo over ten years, although the government changed the definition of “unemployed” during the period. Compare how positivist and Marxist sociologists might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Positivism: official statistics are useful social facts: large-scale, reliable and cheap, they allow trends and correlations to be identified and hypotheses tested (Durkheim). Marxism: official statistics are produced by the state and may serve ruling-class interests, for example by concealing inequality or focusing on working-class crime rather than corporate crime.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “mean”, and give one example.
items.answer: The average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values. Example: the mean of 2, 4 and 9 is 5.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values); 1 mark for a relevant example such as the mean of 2, 4 and 9 is 5. [2]

items.stem: A report on living standards in Singapore uses the mean household income, which is much higher than the median household income, to describe a “typical” family. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: statistical analysis reveals objective patterns and correlations that can be used to test hypotheses and identify causes, as Durkheim did.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Kwame is planning a study of trends in cohabitation and marriage. Explain one strength and one limitation of using official statistics for this study.
items.answer: Strength: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified. Limitation: they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them.
items.markingKey: For each: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in the context of trends in cohabitation and marriage. [4]

items.stem: A study in Accra finds that pupils who eat breakfast get better exam results and concludes that breakfast clubs will close the achievement gap. Explain how interpretivist and positivist sociologists might differ in the way they evaluate this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: statistics only show surface patterns; they need to be interpreted alongside qualitative evidence of meanings, and the categories used are themselves social constructions. Positivism: statistical analysis reveals objective patterns and correlations that can be used to test hypotheses and identify causes, as Durkheim did.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) to research the link between poverty and educational achievement.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they can combine quantitative and qualitative data. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the link between poverty and educational achievement but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes an interview in which the interviewer reads out the same pre-set questions in the same order to every respondent?
items.answer: Structured interview
items.markingKey: Structured interview: an interview in which the interviewer reads out the same pre-set questions in the same order to every respondent. [1]

items.stem: State one way of improving the response rate to a postal or online questionnaire.
items.answer: Include a covering letter explaining the purpose.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. include a covering letter explaining the purpose. [1]

items.stem: Explain Young and Willmott’s argument that families were becoming more symmetrical, based on structured interview evidence, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Young and Willmott used structured interviews with a large sample of families in London to argue that conjugal roles were becoming more equal. Criticism: Oakley criticised their question design: men who did one household task a week counted as “helping”, which exaggerated equality.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Functionalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating experiences of bullying in secondary schools. Explain one limitation of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of experiences of bullying in secondary schools. [2]

items.stem: Daniel is planning a study of experiences of bullying in secondary schools. Explain two limitations of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. 2. Follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to experiences of bullying in secondary schools. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using semi-structured interviews to research attitudes to marriage among young adults in Manila.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; they are more flexible than structured interviews but easier to analyse than unstructured ones. Limitations: follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule; samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying attitudes to marriage among young adults in Manila but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes an experiment carried out in a real-life social setting, often without participants knowing?
items.answer: Field experiment
items.markingKey: Field experiment: an experiment carried out in a real-life social setting, often without participants knowing. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “laboratory experiment” and “independent variable”.
items.answer: Laboratory experiment: an experiment carried out in a controlled, artificial setting where the researcher manipulates variables. Independent variable: the factor the researcher changes to see its effect.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: In a field experiment in Lima, researchers sent 40 pairs of identical job applications to employers. In each pair one used a locally common name and the other a name associated with a minority ethnic group. 20 of the “local-name” applications received an invitation to interview, compared with 12 of the “minority-name” applications. (a) Calculate the percentage of applications in each group that received an interview invitation. (b) Identify the independent and dependent variables in this experiment.
items.answer: (a) Local name: 20 ÷ 40 × 100 = 50%; minority name: 12 ÷ 40 × 100 = 30%. (b) Independent variable: the name (ethnic background) on the application. Dependent variable: whether an interview invitation was received.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each correct percentage. [2] (b) 1 mark each. [2]

items.stem: Kenji, a researcher in Mumbai, sends pairs of identical job applications to employers, one with a local-sounding name and one with a migrant-sounding name. Suggest how an interpretivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: people act on meanings and know when they are being studied, so experiments create artificial behaviour and cannot reveal the meanings behind actions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why field experiments may be more useful to sociologists than laboratory experiments.
items.answer: Natural setting improves validity; participants unaware so no Hawthorne effect; can study real social processes such as discrimination; can study larger groups.

Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Natural setting improves validity; participants unaware so no Hawthorne effect; can study real social processes such as discrimination; can study larger groups. [8]

items.stem: Explain Durkheim’s argument that official suicide statistics can be used comparatively to find the social causes of suicide, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Durkheim compared suicide rates between countries and religious groups, finding rates varied with social integration and regulation. Criticism: Interactionists such as Atkinson argue that coroners’ decisions shape the statistics.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Positivism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Ravi is planning a study of the extent of domestic violence. Explain one strength of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: A sympathetic, non-judgemental interviewer can help people talk about painful or private experiences.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the extent of domestic violence. [2]

items.stem: Official statistics for a region around Colombo show a population of 1,500,000 in both 2010 and 2024. There were 4,800 divorces in 2010 and 5,250 in 2024. (a) Calculate the crude divorce rate (divorces per 1,000 population) for 2010 and for 2024. (b) Explain one reason why official statistics on divorces may be more reliable than official statistics on crime. (c) Suggest two sociological reasons for the change in the crude divorce rate.
items.answer: (a) 2010: 4,800 ÷ 1,500,000 × 1,000 = 3.2; 2024: 5,250 ÷ 1,500,000 × 1,000 = 3.5. (b) Registration of divorces is a legal requirement and the event is clearly defined (a “hard” statistic), whereas crime statistics depend on victims reporting and police recording (“soft” statistics). (c) Changes in divorce law, declining stigma, secularisation, rising expectations of marriage and women’s financial independence.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark both rates correct to 1 d.p. [2] (b) 1 mark: hard vs soft; 1 mark: explanation of registration/definition. [2] (c) 1 mark each valid reason linked to the direction of change. [2]

items.answer: Cheap, available and large-scale; collected regularly so trends can be studied; comparisons between groups and societies; treated as objective social facts; allow hypotheses to be tested (Durkheim).

items.stem: Distinguish between “correlation” and “causation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Correlation: a statistical relationship between two variables, where one changes as the other changes (e.g. areas with higher unemployment tending to have higher crime rates). Causation: a relationship in which a change in one variable directly produces a change in another (e.g. a new law directly reducing a particular crime).

items.answer: Respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify.

items.stem: A research team is investigating trends in cohabitation and marriage. Evaluate the use of official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; positivists see them as objective “social facts” that can be used to test hypotheses. Limitations: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs; definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. items.answer: They are quick to answer, which improves response rates; answers are pre-coded so data is easy to quantify and compare; they are standardised, improving reliability; less risk of researcher interpretation bias.

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying the division of housework in dual-earner families.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: people may report ideal behaviour (for example an equal division of housework) rather than what really happens; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the division of housework in dual-earner families but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. items.stem: Briefly explain Rosenthal and Jacobson’s view that teachers’ expectations can raise pupils’ achievement through a self-fulfilling prophecy.
items.answer: In a field experiment in a Californian school, teachers were told some randomly chosen pupils were “spurters”; many of these pupils made greater IQ gains.

items.stem: In a field experiment in Santiago, researchers sent 200 pairs of identical job applications to employers. In each pair one used a locally common name and the other a name associated with a minority ethnic group. 80 of the “local-name” applications received an invitation to interview, compared with 44 of the “minority-name” applications. (a) Calculate the percentage of applications in each group that received an interview invitation. (b) Identify the independent and dependent variables in this experiment.
items.answer: (a) Local name: 80 ÷ 200 × 100 = 40%; minority name: 44 ÷ 200 × 100 = 22%. (b) Independent variable: the name (ethnic background) on the application. Dependent variable: whether an interview invitation was received.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each correct percentage. [2] (b) 1 mark each. [2]

items.stem: Leila, a researcher in Nairobi, sends pairs of identical job applications to employers, one with a local-sounding name and one with a migrant-sounding name. Suggest how an interpretivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: people act on meanings and know when they are being studied, so experiments create artificial behaviour and cannot reveal the meanings behind actions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Bogotá wants to research the effect of teachers’ expectations on pupils’ progress. Evaluate the use of unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they produce rich, detailed qualitative data that gives verstehen (an empathetic understanding); the interviewee can raise issues the researcher had not thought of, so the research is not limited by pre-set categories. Limitations: the power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear; samples are small, so findings are difficult to generalise. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effect of teachers’ expectations on pupils’ progress but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes data that already exists, collected by someone other than the researcher?
items.answer: Secondary data
items.markingKey: Secondary data: data that already exists, collected by someone other than the researcher. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between hard and soft statistics, using an example of each.
items.answer: Hard statistics are relatively objective and hard to manipulate (e.g. births or deaths); soft statistics depend on interpretation and decisions by officials and can be manipulated (e.g. crime or unemployment figures).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark each example. [4]

items.stem: Kwame uses official unemployment statistics to measure change in Toronto over ten years, although the government changed the definition of “unemployed” during the period. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: official statistics are useful social facts: large-scale, reliable and cheap, they allow trends and correlations to be identified and hypotheses tested (Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Official statistics for a region around Mexico City show a population of 120,000 in both 2010 and 2024. There were 972 marriages in 2010 and 1,068 in 2024. (a) Calculate the crude marriage rate (marriages per 1,000 population) for 2010 and for 2024. (b) Explain one reason why official statistics on marriages may be more reliable than official statistics on crime. (c) Suggest two sociological reasons for the change in the crude marriage rate.
items.answer: (a) 2010: 972 ÷ 120,000 × 1,000 = 8.1; 2024: 1,068 ÷ 120,000 × 1,000 = 8.9. (b) Registration of marriages is a legal requirement and the event is clearly defined (a “hard” statistic), whereas crime statistics depend on victims reporting and police recording (“soft” statistics). (c) Changing attitudes or financial incentives encouraging marriage; a larger number of young adults.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark both rates correct to 1 d.p. [2] (b) 1 mark: hard vs soft; 1 mark: explanation of registration/definition. [2] (c) 1 mark each valid reason linked to the direction of change. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics for studying regional differences in educational achievement.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them; definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying regional differences in educational achievement but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: State one reason why sociologists should be cautious when interpreting statistical data.
items.answer: Statistics may be socially constructed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. statistics may be socially constructed. [1]

items.stem: Explain Durkheim’s argument that statistical patterns in suicide rates reveal the influence of social facts on individual behaviour, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Durkheim identified correlations (e.g. Protestants had higher suicide rates than Catholics) and argued these reflected differences in integration. Criticism: Correlation does not prove causation; differences may reflect how deaths were recorded.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Positivism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A study in Toronto finds that pupils who eat breakfast get better exam results and concludes that breakfast clubs will close the achievement gap. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: statistical analysis reveals objective patterns and correlations that can be used to test hypotheses and identify causes, as Durkheim did.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Mexico City wants to research trends in cohabitation and marriage. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying trends in cohabitation and marriage but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]
